claim: Hippocampal firing is organized in theta sequences controlled by internal memory processes and by external sensory cues.
source: Hippocampal firing is organized in theta sequences controlled by internal memory processes and by external sensory cues, but how these computations are coordinated is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the general context of hippocampal function, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Theta activity is commonly studied as a unique coherent oscillation.
source: Although theta activity is commonly studied as a unique coherent oscillation, it is the result of complex interactions between different rhythm generators.
evidence: This statement describes current research practices in the field, supported by citation context and established knowledge.

claim: Theta activity is the result of complex interactions between different rhythm generators.
source: Although theta activity is commonly studied as a unique coherent oscillation, it is the result of complex interactions between different rhythm generators.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by the experimental data and analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Three different current generators were separated in hippocampal theta activity.
source: Here, by separating hippocampal theta activity in three different current generators, we found epochs with variable theta frequency and phase coupling, suggesting flexible interactions between theta generators.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the ICA analysis and experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Epochs with variable theta frequency and phase coupling suggest flexible interactions between theta generators.
source: Here, by separating hippocampal theta activity in three different current generators, we found epochs with variable theta frequency and phase coupling, suggesting flexible interactions between theta generators.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, based on the data analysis presented in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Epochs of highly synchronized theta rhythmicity preferentially occurred during behavioral tasks requiring coordination between internal memory representations and incoming sensory information.
source: We found that epochs of highly synchronized theta rhythmicity preferentially occurred during behavioral tasks requiring coordination between internal memory representations and incoming sensory information.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Gamma oscillations were associated with specific theta generators.
source: In addition, we found that gamma oscillations were associated with specific theta generators and the strength of theta-gamma coupling predicted the synchronization between theta generators.
evidence: This is supported by the cross-frequency coupling analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The strength of theta-gamma coupling predicted the synchronization between theta generators.
source: In addition, we found that gamma oscillations were associated with specific theta generators and the strength of theta-gamma coupling predicted the synchronization between theta generators.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The hippocampal formation flexibly combines computations subserving spatial navigation driven by external environmental cue stimuli.
source: The hippocampal formation flexibly combines computations subserving spatial navigation, driven by external environmental cue stimuli (McNaughton et al., 1983; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), but also memory processing, dependent on internally generated firing sequences (Pastalkova et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hippocampal formation flexibly combines computations subserving memory processing dependent on internally generated firing sequences.
source: The hippocampal formation flexibly combines computations subserving spatial navigation, driven by external environmental cue stimuli (McNaughton et al., 1983; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), but also memory processing, dependent on internally generated firing sequences (Pastalkova et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Oscillatory activity patterns in brain networks have been proposed as a mechanism to organize different computations.
source: The characteristic oscillatory activity patterns in brain networks have been proposed as a mechanism to organize different computations and, depending on the cognitive needs, integrate or segregated them in oscillatory cycles (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Engel et al., 2001; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Theta and gamma oscillations are the most prominent rhythms recorded in freely moving animals in the hippocampus.
source: In the hippocampus, theta and gamma oscillations are the most prominent rhythms recorded in freely moving animals (Buzsáki, 2002; Colgin, 2016; Colgin, 2013; Vanderwolf, 1969).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established research.

claim: The processing of environmental cues and the encoding of memories have been associated with the input from the entorhinal cortex arriving at CA1 at a particular phase of the theta cycle.
source: Theoretical and experimental work in the hippocampus have associated the processing of environmental cues and the encoding of memories with the input from the entorhinal cortex (EC) arriving at CA1 at a particular phase of the theta cycle, and the retrieval of memories with the CA3 output to CA1 in a different phase of the cycle (Douchamps et al., 2013; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: The retrieval of memories has been associated with the CA3 output to CA1 in a different phase of the theta cycle.
source: Theoretical and experimental work in the hippocampus have associated the processing of environmental cues and the encoding of memories with the input from the entorhinal cortex (EC) arriving at CA1 at a particular phase of the theta cycle, and the retrieval of memories with the CA3 output to CA1 in a different phase of the cycle (Douchamps et al., 2013; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Information transmission between hippocampal regions is proposed to occur in gamma oscillations of different frequencies organized in the phase of the slower CA1 theta rhythm.
source: Information transmission between these regions is proposed to occur in gamma oscillations of different frequencies organized in the phase of the slower CA1 theta rhythm (Colgin et al., 2009; Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Theta-gamma associations are known as cross-frequency coupling (CFC).
source: These theta-gamma associations, known as cross-frequency coupling (CFC), are modulated during exploration and memory-guided behaviors (Cabral et al., 2014; Canolty et al., 2006; Colgin, 2015; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014; Tort et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a definition of a technical term used in the field.

claim: Cross-frequency coupling is modulated during exploration and memory-guided behaviors.
source: These theta-gamma associations, known as cross-frequency coupling (CFC), are modulated during exploration and memory-guided behaviors (Cabral et al., 2014; Canolty et al., 2006; Colgin, 2015; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014; Tort et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Theta-gamma interaction may vary in a cycle-by-cycle manner within a global hippocampal theta rhythmicity.
source: Recent studies have further shown that theta-gamma interaction may vary in a cycle-by-cycle manner within a global hippocampal theta rhythmicity (Dvorak et al., 2018; Lopes-Dos-Santos et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Theta oscillations originating in different anatomical layers of the hippocampus are known to coexist.
source: However, theta oscillations originating in different anatomical layers of the hippocampus are known to coexist (Alonso and García-Austt, 1987; Bland and Whishaw, 1976; Buzsáki, 2002; Charpak et al., 1995; Green and Rawlins, 1979; Vanderwolf C et al., 1973; Kramis et al., 1975; Montgomery et al., 2009; Vanderwolf, 1969; Winson, 1974) and, therefore, theta-gamma interactions need to be interpreted in the context of multiple rhythm generators.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Important rhythm generators are located in EC layers II and III.
source: In addition to the classical medial septum/diagonal band of Broca input imposing a global rhythmicity to the hippocampus and EC, important rhythm generators are located in EC layers II (EC2) and III (EC3), whose activity reach the dentate gyrus (DG) and hippocampus proper through the perforant and temporoammonic pathways, respectively, and from CA3 activity reaching CA1 stratum radiatum through the Schafer collaterals (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This is anatomical and functional knowledge supported by citation.

claim: EC2 activity reaches the dentate gyrus and hippocampus proper through the perforant pathway.
source: In addition to the classical medial septum/diagonal band of Broca input imposing a global rhythmicity to the hippocampus and EC, important rhythm generators are located in EC layers II (EC2) and III (EC3), whose activity reach the dentate gyrus (DG) and hippocampus proper through the perforant and temporoammonic pathways, respectively, and from CA3 activity reaching CA1 stratum radiatum through the Schafer collaterals (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: EC3 activity reaches the dentate gyrus and hippocampus proper through the temporoammonic pathway.
source: In addition to the classical medial septum/diagonal band of Broca input imposing a global rhythmicity to the hippocampus and EC, important rhythm generators are located in EC layers II (EC2) and III (EC3), whose activity reach the dentate gyrus (DG) and hippocampus proper through the perforant and temporoammonic pathways, respectively, and from CA3 activity reaching CA1 stratum radiatum through the Schafer collaterals (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CA3 activity reaches CA1 stratum radiatum through the Schaffer collaterals.
source: In addition to the classical medial septum/diagonal band of Broca input imposing a global rhythmicity to the hippocampus and EC, important rhythm generators are located in EC layers II (EC2) and III (EC3), whose activity reach the dentate gyrus (DG) and hippocampus proper through the perforant and temporoammonic pathways, respectively, and from CA3 activity reaching CA1 stratum radiatum through the Schafer collaterals (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Theta oscillations in the hippocampus are most commonly studied as a unique coherent oscillation across hippocampal layers.
source: Importantly, although theta oscillations in the hippocampus are most commonly studied as a unique coherent oscillation across hippocampal layers, exhibiting a characteristic amplitude/phase vs. depth variation (Buzsáki, 2002), the frequency and phase of the CA3 theta rhythm generator was shown to change relatively independently from the EC theta inputs (Kocsis et al., 1999; Montgomery et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes common research practice, supported by citation and knowledge of the field.

claim: The frequency and phase of the CA3 theta rhythm generator was shown to change relatively independently from the EC theta inputs.
source: Importantly, although theta oscillations in the hippocampus are most commonly studied as a unique coherent oscillation across hippocampal layers, exhibiting a characteristic amplitude/phase vs. depth variation (Buzsáki, 2002), the frequency and phase of the CA3 theta rhythm generator was shown to change relatively independently from the EC theta inputs (Kocsis et al., 1999; Montgomery et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different theta oscillations may represent different theta-gamma coding frameworks.
source: One appealing possibility is that different theta oscillations may represent different theta-gamma coding frameworks, providing the substrate to segregate, but also to integrate computations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their interpretation of the literature.

claim: High density electrophysiological recordings aided by source separation techniques were used to characterize the dynamic properties of three different theta and three different gamma dipoles in the hippocampus.
source: Using high density electrophysiological recordings aided by source separation techniques we characterized the dynamic properties of three different theta and three different gamma dipoles in the hippocampus with origins in the CA3 Schaffer collateral layer, the EC3 projection to the stratum lacunosum-moleculare and the EC2 projection to the mid-molecular layer of the DG, respectively, and found strong support for the existence of different theta-gamma frameworks.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Three different theta dipoles have origins in the CA3 Schaffer collateral layer, the EC3 projection to the stratum lacunosum-moleculare and the EC2 projection to the mid-molecular layer of the DG.
source: Using high density electrophysiological recordings aided by source separation techniques we characterized the dynamic properties of three different theta and three different gamma dipoles in the hippocampus with origins in the CA3 Schaffer collateral layer, the EC3 projection to the stratum lacunosum-moleculare and the EC2 projection to the mid-molecular layer of the DG, respectively, and found strong support for the existence of different theta-gamma frameworks.
evidence: This is a finding from the ICA analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Strong support was found for the existence of different theta-gamma frameworks.
source: Using high density electrophysiological recordings aided by source separation techniques we characterized the dynamic properties of three different theta and three different gamma dipoles in the hippocampus with origins in the CA3 Schaffer collateral layer, the EC3 projection to the stratum lacunosum-moleculare and the EC2 projection to the mid-molecular layer of the DG, respectively, and found strong support for the existence of different theta-gamma frameworks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Optogenetic tools targeted to CA3 parvalbumin interneurons show the specific modulation of the CA3-associated vs. the EC-associated theta generators.
source: Using optogenetic tools targeted to CA3 parvalbumin interneurons, we show the specific modulation of the CA3-associated vs. the EC-associated theta generators, demonstrating independent theta oscillations in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Independent theta oscillations exist in the hippocampus.
source: Using optogenetic tools targeted to CA3 parvalbumin interneurons, we show the specific modulation of the CA3-associated vs. the EC-associated theta generators, demonstrating independent theta oscillations in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study, supported by the optogenetic experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Phase shifts between the identified theta frameworks served to coordinate them in pairs or triads, in a sub-second timescale.
source: Nevertheless, phase shifts between the identified theta frameworks served to coordinate them in pairs or triads, in a sub-second timescale.
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICPC analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pathway-specific gamma oscillations consistently precede theta phase shifts.
source: We then characterized theta-gamma interactions between the different pathways and established an association with the synchronization state in the hippocampal network. Theta-gamma CFC was stronger during higher theta synchronization and we found that pathway-specific gamma oscillations consistently precede theta phase shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFD analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Theta-gamma CFC was stronger during higher theta synchronization.
source: We then characterized theta-gamma interactions between the different pathways and established an association with the synchronization state in the hippocampal network. Theta-gamma CFC was stronger during higher theta synchronization and we found that pathway-specific gamma oscillations consistently precede theta phase shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both theta-gamma CFC and the coordination between theta oscillations were consistently higher during mismatch novelty and memory guided decisions.
source: We found that both, theta-gamma CFC and the coordination between theta oscillations, were consistently higher during mismatch novelty and memory guided decisions, in situations in which the representation of the context from memory is compared against the incoming sensory information.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings were performed using linear array electrodes across the dorsal hippocampus in five rats.
source: We performed electrophysiological recordings using linear array electrodes across the dorsal hippocampus in five rats (see Materials and methods, Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Recordings were carried out while the animal freely explored a familiar open field.
source: Recordings were carried out while the animal freely explored a familiar open field (Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), a novel open field (Figure 6) or a T-maze (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Three robust components were dissected in all subjects using spatial discrimination techniques based on independent component analysis.
source: Using spatial discrimination techniques to separate LFP sources contributed by different synaptic pathways, based on independent component analysis (ICA, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Benito et al., 2014; Fernández-Ruiz and Herreras, 2013; Herreras, 2016; Herreras et al., 2015; Lęski et al., 2010; Makarov et al., 2010; Makarova et al., 2011; Ortuño et al., 2019; Schomburg et al., 2014), we dissected three robust components in all subjects (Figure 1; Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology and results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The maximum voltages and dipoles in the current source density depth profiles of the three components matched the stratified distribution of known terminal fields in the hippocampus.
source: The maximum voltages (Figure 1b) and dipoles in the current source density (CSD) depth profiles (Figure 1c) of the three components matched the stratified distribution of known terminal fields in the hippocampus and the currents resulting from stimulation of the corresponding pathways, as previously shown (Benito et al., 2014; Fernández-Ruiz and Herreras, 2013; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1b and 1c, and by citations to previous work.

claim: The first component was located in the stratum radiatum, where the CA3 Schaffer collateral/commissural pathway targets the CA1 region.
source: The first component was located in the stratum radiatum, where the CA3 Schaffer collateral/commissural pathway targets the CA1 region (labelled as Schaffer component or Sch-IC).
evidence: This is a finding from the ICA analysis shown in Figure 1, supported by anatomical knowledge.

claim: The second component matched the EC3 projection in the stratum lacunosum-moleculare.
source: The second matched the EC3 projection in the stratum lacunosum-moleculare (lm-IC), and the third one the perforant pathway from EC2 to the mid-molecular layer of the DG (PP-IC).
evidence: This is a finding from the ICA analysis shown in Figure 1, supported by anatomical knowledge.

claim: The third component matched the perforant pathway from EC2 to the mid-molecular layer of the DG.
source: The second matched the EC3 projection in the stratum lacunosum-moleculare (lm-IC), and the third one the perforant pathway from EC2 to the mid-molecular layer of the DG (PP-IC).
evidence: This is a finding from the ICA analysis shown in Figure 1, supported by anatomical knowledge.

claim: The three components represent the synaptic contributions with distinct anatomical origins recorded in the LFP.
source: These three components, referred to as pathway-specific LFPs or IC-LFPs, represent the synaptic contributions with distinct anatomical origins recorded in the LFP (Herreras, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ICA results, supported by citation to methodological work.

claim: The power spectra of IC-LFPs exhibited a clear peak at theta frequency and broadband gamma activity.
source: The power spectra of these signals exhibited a clear peak at theta frequency (6–10 Hz) and broadband gamma activity (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: CA3 and EC3 neurons have been shown to fire phase locked to discrete gamma band oscillations in the downstream Sch-IC and lm-IC, respectively.
source: CA3 and EC3 neurons have been shown to fire phase locked to discrete gamma band oscillations in the downstream Sch-IC and lm-IC, respectively (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2012a; Schomburg et al., 2014), with gamma oscillations segregated in the phases of the theta wave recorded in CA1 (Colgin et al., 2009; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gamma oscillations are segregated in the phases of the theta wave recorded in CA1.
source: CA3 and EC3 neurons have been shown to fire phase locked to discrete gamma band oscillations in the downstream Sch-IC and lm-IC, respectively (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2012a; Schomburg et al., 2014), with gamma oscillations segregated in the phases of the theta wave recorded in CA1 (Colgin et al., 2009; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pathway-specific gamma activities were distributed in the theta cycle, with lm-IC close to the theta peak and followed by Sch-IC.
source: In good agreement, pathway-specific gamma activities were distributed in the theta cycle, with lm-IC close to the theta peak (π radians) and followed by Sch-IC (Figure 1f), showing consistency with the firing properties of principal neurons in their respective upstream afferent layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Entorhinal principal cells in EC2 and EC3 were shown to fire in anti-phase, relative to the theta oscillation.
source: Similarly, entorhinal principal cells in EC2 and EC3 were shown to fire in anti-phase, relative to the theta oscillation (Mizuseki et al., 2009) and, accordingly, large amplitude gamma oscillations in PP-IC and lm-IC in our recordings were found shifted 180° (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Large amplitude gamma oscillations in PP-IC and lm-IC were found shifted 180°.
source: Similarly, entorhinal principal cells in EC2 and EC3 were shown to fire in anti-phase, relative to the theta oscillation (Mizuseki et al., 2009) and, accordingly, large amplitude gamma oscillations in PP-IC and lm-IC in our recordings were found shifted 180° (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: All IC-LFPs exhibited prominent coherence with the LFP signal mainly in the theta range.
source: All IC-LFPs exhibited prominent coherence with the LFP signal mainly in the theta range (and its first harmonic, Figure 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the coherence analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The coherence at theta frequency was high between IC-LFP pairs.
source: Similarly, the coherence at theta frequency was high between IC-LFP pairs (0.41, 0.31, 0.61, for Sch-lm, Sch-PP and lm-PP, respectively, Figure 1g), being larger between EC-associated generators (p<0.0001, ANOVA with degrees of freedom corrected by Greenhouse-Geisser, F(1.091, 4.363)=89.33).
evidence: This claim is supported by the coherence analysis shown in Figure 1g, with statistical testing.

claim: Coherence was larger between EC-associated generators.
source: Similarly, the coherence at theta frequency was high between IC-LFP pairs (0.41, 0.31, 0.61, for Sch-lm, Sch-PP and lm-PP, respectively, Figure 1g), being larger between EC-associated generators (p<0.0001, ANOVA with degrees of freedom corrected by Greenhouse-Geisser, F(1.091, 4.363)=89.33).
evidence: This claim is supported by the coherence analysis shown in Figure 1g, with statistical testing.

claim: Higher coherence was found between raw LFPs at different frequency bands compared to IC-LFPs, likely due to volume conduction between channels.
source: This comparison revealed higher coherence between raw LFPs at different frequency bands, likely due to volume conduction between channels, not present in the IC-LFPs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coherence comparison shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Theta coherence was significantly lower between IC-LFPs in the stratum radiatum compared to raw LFPs.
source: For the theta band, the differences were most evident in the stratum radiatum, where theta coherence was significantly lower between IC-LFPs (Figure 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the coherence comparison shown in Figure 1g.

claim: ICA allows the separation of sources, even if there is a high coherence between them.
source: Note at this point that the extraction of highly coherent signals is perfectly compatible with ICA. This methodology finds components that are spatially distributed, and only requires small differences in their temporal co-variation (i.e. temporal jitter and/or amplitude variation). Therefore, ICA allows the separation of sources, even if there is a high coherence between them (Makarova et al., 2011; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological explanation supported by citation.

claim: All IC-LFPs showed significant coupling in the theta range with the reference LFP signal.
source: The coherence results were confirmed by the ICPC analysis, demonstrating a significant coupling in the theta range with the reference LFP signal (ICPC = 0.50/0.73/0.61 for Sch-IC/lm-IC/PP-IC vs. CA1 LFP, respectively, p<0.0001, surrogate test), which also showed the characteristic phase shift across layers (π/2, 0.8π and 1.1π radians for Sch-IC, lm-IC and PP-IC, respectively; Figure 1h).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICPC analysis shown in Figure 1h, with statistical testing.

claim: IC-LFPs showed characteristic phase shifts across layers.
source: The coherence results were confirmed by the ICPC analysis, demonstrating a significant coupling in the theta range with the reference LFP signal (ICPC = 0.50/0.73/0.61 for Sch-IC/lm-IC/PP-IC vs. CA1 LFP, respectively, p<0.0001, surrogate test), which also showed the characteristic phase shift across layers (π/2, 0.8π and 1.1π radians for Sch-IC, lm-IC and PP-IC, respectively; Figure 1h).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICPC analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The lack of coherence closer to the unit between theta oscillations in the IC-LFPs suggests the coexistence of different theta current generators with certain degree of independency.
source: Interestingly, the lack of coherence closer to the unit between theta oscillations in the IC-LFPs was already suggesting the coexistence of different theta current generators with certain degree of independency, rather than the artificial breakdown of a unique theta rhythm into spatially segregated components.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coherence results.

claim: A transgenic rat cre line expressing Cre recombinase under the rat parvalbumin promoter was used.
source: Using a transgenic rat cre line (LE-TG[Pvalb-iCre]2Ottc, NIDA, USA) and adeno-associated virus (AAV1-EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP-WPRE-hGH, Penn Vector Core, USA) injected in the dorsal CA3 (Figure 2a), we expressed the excitatory Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in parvalbumin positive (PV+) interneurons (Figure 2b, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Channelrhodopsin-2 was expressed in parvalbumin positive interneurons in dorsal CA3.
source: Using a transgenic rat cre line (LE-TG[Pvalb-iCre]2Ottc, NIDA, USA) and adeno-associated virus (AAV1-EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP-WPRE-hGH, Penn Vector Core, USA) injected in the dorsal CA3 (Figure 2a), we expressed the excitatory Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in parvalbumin positive (PV+) interneurons (Figure 2b, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and is confirmed by the immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Blue light illumination in animals freely-exploring an open field significantly and specifically decreased the power of theta in the Sch-IC.
source: As shown in Figure 2c–d, blue light illumination (460 nm) in animals freely-exploring an open field significantly and specifically decreased the power of theta in the Sch-IC and the corresponding pathway-specific low gamma oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Blue light illumination significantly decreased the corresponding pathway-specific low gamma oscillations in Sch-IC.
source: As shown in Figure 2c–d, blue light illumination (460 nm) in animals freely-exploring an open field significantly and specifically decreased the power of theta in the Sch-IC and the corresponding pathway-specific low gamma oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: The oscillatory activities in lm-IC and PP-IC were preserved during blue light illumination.
source: In contrast, the oscillatory activities (power and peak frequency) in lm-IC and PP-IC were preserved (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The modulation of theta power specifically in the Sch-IC with the preservation of peak theta frequencies in the three generators demonstrated the existence of independent theta oscillators in CA3 and EC.
source: The modulation of theta power specifically in the Sch-IC with the preservation of peak theta frequencies in the three generators, conclusively demonstrated the existence of independent theta oscillators in CA3 and EC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Theta interactions between pathways were not constant in time, but presented periods of high and low synchronization.
source: As expected from the results in Figure 1g and h, theta interactions between pathways were not constant in time, but presented periods of high and low synchronization (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The distribution of the ICPC over all animals showed a peak close to perfect phase locking, but with an important tail of low-synchronized epochs.
source: The distribution of the ICPC over all animals showed a peak close to perfect phase locking, but with an important tail of low-synchronized epochs, with approximately the 20% of the cycles presenting an ICPC lower than 0.8.
evidence: This is a description of the ICPC distribution shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Approximately 20% of the cycles presented an ICPC lower than 0.8.
source: The distribution of the ICPC over all animals showed a peak close to perfect phase locking, but with an important tail of low-synchronized epochs, with approximately the 20% of the cycles presenting an ICPC lower than 0.8.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the ICPC analysis.

claim: The highest synchronization was found between PP-IC and lm-IC.
source: Again, the highest synchronization was found between PP-IC and lm-IC, in agreement with the coherence analyses (Figure 1g) and consistent with the likely origin of these generators in two sublayers of the same cortical regions (EC).
evidence: This is a finding from the ICPC analysis, consistent with the coherence results.

claim: ICPC from raw LFP signals showed significantly higher estimates of phase coupling than for IC-LFPs.
source: As we did for the coherence analysis, we also computed the ICPC from the raw LFP signals recorded at str. radiatum, lacunosum-moleculare and hilus. This analysis showed significantly higher estimates of phase coupling based on LFPs than for IC-LFPs (averaged ICPC = 0.88/0.93 for the three IC-LFPs/raw LFPs, p<0.01, paired t-test, t = 5.35, N = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of ICPC values between IC-LFPs and raw LFPs, with statistical testing.

claim: Perfect phase locking was strongly reduced in IC-LFP signals, unveiling the spurious coupling measured on the raw LFPs likely due to the mixture of sources by volume conduction.
source: Perfect phase locking (ICPC = 1) was strongly reduced in IC-LFP signals, unveiling the spurious coupling measured on the raw LFPs likely due to the mixture of sources by volume conduction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ICPC comparison between IC-LFPs and raw LFPs.

claim: The coupling strength between consecutive cycles spreads on a time scale in the order of one second.
source: These results provided a monotonously rising curve up to 0.75 s; from there on, the curve hardly increased. This indicates that the coupling strength between consecutive cycles spreads on a time scale in the order of one second, thus expecting dynamical changes in the ICPC in this time scale.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics analysis shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The coexistence of different temporal frames in the theta range opens the possibility to multiple theta-gamma interactions.
source: The above results supported the coexistence of different temporal frames in the theta range to organize hippocampal activity. Thus, since gamma activity is nested to the theta cycle, it opened the possibility to multiple theta-gamma interactions (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the previous findings.

claim: Conventional theta-gamma phase-amplitude CFC analysis identified the typical coupling between CA1 theta and a slow gamma band of CA3 origin.
source: This analysis identified the typical coupling between CA1 theta and a slow gamma band of CA3 origin (Sch-IC; maximal modulation at 37.5 ± 5 Hz; Colgin et al., 2009; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014) and a medium gamma band of EC3 origin (lm-IC; 82.5 ± 4 Hz medium gamma; Colgin et al., 2009; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFC analysis shown in Figure 3b and citations to previous work.

claim: Conventional theta-gamma phase-amplitude CFC analysis identified a medium gamma band of EC3 origin.
source: This analysis identified the typical coupling between CA1 theta and a slow gamma band of CA3 origin (Sch-IC; maximal modulation at 37.5 ± 5 Hz; Colgin et al., 2009; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014) and a medium gamma band of EC3 origin (lm-IC; 82.5 ± 4 Hz medium gamma; Colgin et al., 2009; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFC analysis shown in Figure 3b and citations to previous work.

claim: The analysis revealed an additional theta-nested fast gamma band in the mid-molecular layer of the DG overlapping the terminal field of EC2 inputs.
source: The analysis also revealed an additional theta-nested fast gamma band (130 ± 10 Hz,) in the mid-molecular layer of the DG overlapping the terminal field of EC2 inputs, compatible with the previously found theta-gamma CFC in the DG (Bragin et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a new finding from the CFC analysis, consistent with previous work cited.

claim: Stronger theta-gamma CFC was systematically observed in IC-LFPs vs. LFPs.
source: The key new finding was the systematic observation of stronger theta-gamma CFC in IC-LFPs vs. LFPs (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFC comparison shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The theta oscillation recorded in the LFP and typically used as a reference in CFC analysis is a mixture of different theta generators of variable coherence.
source: The result was not totally unexpected, since we had found that the theta oscillation recorded in the LFP and typically used as a reference in CFC analysis was indeed a mixture of different theta generators of variable coherence (see Figure 2d–e above).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the previous findings in Figure 2.

claim: Theta power in all IC-LFPs correlated with the ICPC, with larger theta power associated with states of higher synchronization.
source: We found that theta power in all IC-LFPs correlated with the ICPC, with larger theta power associated with states of higher synchronization (Figure 4a, b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The frequency of the theta oscillation was constant across synchronization states in the Sch-IC.
source: Interestingly, the frequency of the theta oscillation was constant across synchronization states in the Sch-IC, but varied in the two EC-associated generators (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Theta frequencies in lm-IC and PP-IC increased with ICPC.
source: Theta frequencies in lm-IC and PP-IC increased with ICPC (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: Narrowband gamma power correlated with the ICPC in lm-IC, but not in Sch-IC nor PP-IC.
source: Regarding gamma activity, broadband power did not correlate with theta synchronization (not shown), in contrast to narrowband power (slow/medium/fast gamma for Sch-IC/lm-IC/PP-IC, respectively), which correlated with the ICPC in lm-IC, but not in Sch-IC nor PP-IC (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Multiple linear regression analysis demonstrated the main effect of theta power on the ICPC value.
source: The result demonstrated the main effect of theta power on the ICPC value, with a lower, but significant, contribution of theta frequency and running speed (Figure 4c, p<0.05, t-test against zero between beta values of each factor, Bonferroni corrected, Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the multiple linear regression analysis shown in Figure 4c, with statistical testing.

claim: There was a striking correlation between the CFC and theta synchronization.
source: Finally, this analysis unveiled a striking correlation between the CFC and theta synchronization (Figure 4b and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b and d.

claim: Strong theta-gamma modulation was associated with high ICPC values.
source: Strong theta-gamma modulation was associated with high ICPC values, while weak or nearly absent CFC was found in periods of low synchronization.
evidence: This is a description of the correlation between CFC and ICPC shown in Figure 4.

claim: Within-pathway CFC was associated to the synchronization between pathways.
source: This result indicated that within-pathway CFC was associated to the synchronization between pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between CFC and ICPC.

claim: CFD resulted in negative values for the specific gamma bands nested to the theta oscillations in the corresponding IC-LFPs.
source: As shown in Figure 5a for the group data, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for individual animals, CFD resulted in negative values (amplitude-phase coupling, APC) for the specific gamma bands nested to the theta oscillations in the corresponding IC-LFPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFD analysis shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gamma amplitude to theta phase directionality is given by the consistent anticipation of the gamma activity to the theta phase.
source: This gamma amplitude to theta phase directionality is given by the consistent anticipation of the gamma activity to the theta phase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CFD results.

claim: Negative values of CFD were found in the LFPs in str. lacunosum-moleculare and in the DG, supporting the driving role of gamma oscillations over the phase of the theta waves.
source: Negative values of CFD were found in the LFPs in str. lacunosum-moleculare and in the DG, supporting the driving role of gamma oscillations over the phase of the theta waves.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFD analysis on raw LFPs shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The absolute value of the CFD was higher using IC-LFPs than LFPs.
source: We could not find a significant directionality in the case of the str. radiatum LFP and, in all cases, the absolute value of the CFD was higher using IC-LFPs than LFPs (Figure 5d), demonstrating that source-separation tools outperform the use of raw LFPs to investigate pathway interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of CFD values shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Source-separation tools outperform the use of raw LFPs to investigate pathway interactions.
source: We could not find a significant directionality in the case of the str. radiatum LFP and, in all cases, the absolute value of the CFD was higher using IC-LFPs than LFPs (Figure 5d), demonstrating that source-separation tools outperform the use of raw LFPs to investigate pathway interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of CFD values between IC-LFPs and raw LFPs.

claim: The neuronal circuits supporting gamma oscillations in the hippocampus set the timing of principal cells activity in the theta range.
source: Overall, our CFD analysis suggests that the neuronal circuits supporting gamma oscillations in the hippocampus set the timing of principal cells activity in the theta range, as reflected in the phase of the recorded theta oscillations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CFD results.

claim: Both CFC and inter-regional coherence independently correlate with learning.
source: Previous studies have shown that both CFC and inter-regional coherence, independently, correlate with learning (Canolty et al., 2006; Engel et al., 2001; Fries, 2015; Fries, 2005; Palva et al., 2005; Tort et al., 2009; Tort et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Layer-specific interactions would phase-lock theta oscillations between layers to facilitate the integration of CA3-mediated and EC-mediated information streams in CA1.
source: More specifically, we hypothesized that layer-specific interactions would phase-lock theta oscillations between layers to facilitate the integration of CA3-mediated and EC-mediated information streams in CA1; for instance, in learning conditions requiring the comparison of context representations from memory (Sch-IC pathway) and from the environment (lm-IC and PP-IC pathways; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Dudai and Morris, 2013; Wang and Morris, 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Mismatch novelty is a learning condition in which the subject is re-exposed to a previously visited context which has been modified.
source: One such learning conditions is mismatch novelty (Lever et al., 2006), in which the subject is re-exposed to a previously visited context which has been modified.
evidence: This is a definition of the behavioral paradigm, supported by citation.

claim: When the animal entered the arena, the ICPC between theta oscillations was high and comparable in both control and novelty conditions during the first two minutes of exploration.
source: When the animal entered the arena, the ICPC between theta oscillations was high and comparable in both conditions during the first two minutes of exploration (Figure 6b, t1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Synchronization remained high during novelty but rapidly decayed in the known environment as the animal explored the context.
source: As the animal explored the context, synchronization remained high during novelty, but rapidly decayed in the known environment (Figure 6b, t2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: By the end of the exploration time both control and novelty conditions decreased to the same level of theta synchronization.
source: Consistent with the notion of information transmission to update an existing memory, by the end of the exploration time both conditions decreased to the same level of theta synchronization (Figure 6b, t3), when the introduced tactile stimulus had lost its novelty.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: There were no differences in movement velocity between novelty and habituation sessions.
source: As a control, we tested locomotor activity comparing movement velocity between novelty and habituation sessions (Figure 6c), without finding differences between sessions (p>0.3, t-test, Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the velocity comparison shown in Figure 6c, with statistical testing.

claim: Theta power and the experimental condition are the main factors that contribute to the ICPC value in the mismatch novelty task.
source: We found that theta power and the experimental condition are the main factors that contribute to the ICPC value, with other variables such us running speed and time marginally contributing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multiple linear regression analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The CFC index paralleled the changes in theta synchronization during the complete session in both control and novelty conditions.
source: We then computed the CFC index (MI) in the same recordings and found that it paralleled the changes in theta synchronization during the complete session in both conditions, as shown in Figure 6b and e.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFC analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The CFC strength was higher in the three IC-LFPs during the novelty sessions associated with the higher theta synchronization.
source: The CFC strength was higher in the three IC-LFPs during the novelty sessions associated with the higher theta synchronization, and decreased towards the end of the session in parallel with the ICPC (Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFC analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The increased theta synchronization between the three IC-LFPs was maintained during novelty in the absence of rearing epochs.
source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1, the increased theta synchronization between the three IC-LFPs was maintained during novelty in the absence of rearing epochs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The changes found in mismatch novelty cannot be solely explained by the rearing behavior.
source: We concluded that the changes found in mismatch novelty cannot be solely explained by the rearing behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis after removing rearing epochs.

claim: Significantly increased CFC was found in the central arm for the three IC-LFPs in the T-maze task.
source: We found significantly increased CFC in the central arm for the three IC-LFPs (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CFC analysis in the T-maze task shown in Figure 7c, with statistical testing.

claim: An increase in theta ICPC was found in the central arm during the same epochs as increased CFC in the T-maze task.
source: Importantly, concomitant with CFC, we also found an increase in theta ICPC in the central arm during the same epochs (Figure 7d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICPC analysis in the T-maze task shown in Figure 7d and e.

claim: The results of the two behavioral tasks demonstrate that theta-gamma CFC and theta ICPC across generators are linked.
source: The results of the two behavioral tasks, thus, demonstrate that theta-gamma CFC and theta ICPC across generators are linked and preferentially occur during memory-guided exploration and mismatch novelty detection, two conditions in which internally generated memory representations need to be integrated with the incoming sensory information about external cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral experiments in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Theta-gamma CFC and theta ICPC preferentially occur during memory-guided exploration and mismatch novelty detection.
source: The results of the two behavioral tasks, thus, demonstrate that theta-gamma CFC and theta ICPC across generators are linked and preferentially occur during memory-guided exploration and mismatch novelty detection, two conditions in which internally generated memory representations need to be integrated with the incoming sensory information about external cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral experiments in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Different theta-gamma frameworks may flexibly coordinate information transmission in the hippocampus.
source: They support the idea that different theta-gamma frameworks may flexibly coordinate information transmission in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the experimental findings in the study.
